49.0.s.en: 1. Praise of Josiah the righteous king

49.0.0.en: 1 The remembrance of Josiah is like the composition of the perfume that is made by the art of the apothecary. 2 It is sweet as honey in every mouth, and as music at a banquet of wine. 3 He was appointed to turn the people to repentance by his hand; and he took away the abominations of iniquity. 4 He directed his heart unto the Lord, and in the days of the ungodly he established godliness.

49.0.1.en: The remembrance of Josiah is like a composition of incense prepared by the art of the apothecary; it is sweet in every mouth like honey, and like music at a banquet of wine [1].

49.0.2.en: No godly king, a man of faith, was found in the seventh century B.C. except Josiah, the great reformer who reigned in Jerusalem from 640 B.C. until his death in the battle of Megiddo in 609 B.C.

49.0.3.en: Jeroboam the son of Nebat was a byword for evil, and Josiah was a byword for the removal of idols (2 Kgs 22-23; 2 Chr 35:1-6).

49.0.4.en: The use of music at tables of food is an expression of the spirit of joy, as it was used in the parable of the son who returned to his father (Lk 15). It was as though Josiah, by his walk in the Lord, were sending forth joy and gladness into the life of the believers.

49.1.0.en: He led in the turning of the people, and he rooted out the abominations of iniquity [2].

49.1.1.en: Like the writers of Kings and Chronicles, Ben Sira took note of his great role in purifying the Promised Land from idolatry [2]. Ben Sira did not mention the discovery of the Law in the Temple in 622 B.C. (2 Kgs 22:3-13; 2 Chr 34:14-21). Ben Sira highlighted the difficulty of the work in the time of Josiah, since he lived in an atmosphere of great corruption, and his age was called "the days of iniquity."

49.2.0.en: And he directed his heart to the Lord; and in the days of iniquity he strengthened godliness [3].

49.3.s.en: 2. The wicked kings of Judah and the Babylonian captivity

49.3.0.en: 5 All except David and Hezekiah and Josiah were guilty of transgression. 6 They forsook the law of the Most High. The kings of Judah failed. 7 They gave their horn unto others, and their glory to a strange nation. 8 They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary, and made her streets desolate, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah. 9 For they entreated him evil, who yet was sanctified in the womb a prophet, to root out, and to afflict, and to destroy; and likewise to build up and to plant.

49.3.1.en: They all sinned one after another, except David, Hezekiah and Josiah, for they forsook the law of the Most High. The kings of Judah failed [4].

49.3.2.en: Josiah was worthy to be counted with David and Hezekiah, for the three were kings distinguished by godliness and faith.

49.3.3.en: The secret of the corruption of the kings of Judah was their forsaking of the Law, and consequently they did not cleave to God; so God allowed the chastening of Judah through the fall of Jerusalem into the Babylonian captivity in 587 B.C.

49.3.4.en: For they gave their power to others, and their glory to a strange nation [5].

49.4.0.en: (The enemies) burned with fire the chosen city, the city of the sanctuary, and made her streets desolate [6].

49.4.1.en: Jerusalem was exposed to ruin, and her streets became as a wilderness, and the enemies also defiled the Temple and destroyed it.

49.5.0.en: According to the word of Jeremiah, they entreated him evil, who was sanctified as a prophet while he was still in his mother's womb, to pluck up, to destroy and to ruin, and likewise to build up and to plant [7].

49.5.1.en: Ben Sira calls us to read the Lamentations of Jeremiah, which he wrote when he saw destruction come upon the city and the people, and the princes, the nobles and the gifted were led into captivity in 587 B.C.

49.5.2.en: The prophet who was linked to King Josiah is Jeremiah, whose prophetic ministry extended even after the fall of Judah into the Babylonian captivity. Each of them was in bitterness because of the spiritual corruption of the kingdom of Judah. It seems that they both failed in the spiritual reform of the kingdom, yet both remain great in the eyes of God because of their zeal and their striving.

49.5.3.en: King Josiah died in the battle of Megiddo against Pharaoh, when he tried to support Babylon against Pharaoh, and in less than 20 years Babylon laid Jerusalem waste, and Jeremiah was killed in Egypt, in the land from which Moses had come out with the people to lead them across into the wilderness and to enter the Promised Land.

49.5.4.en: The prophecies of the prophet Jeremiah are full of sorrow, since the time of the Babylonian captivity was drawing near while the leaders and the people treated the matter lightly and with contempt. This was a burden on his soul. He tried to keep silent but could not (Jer 20:9). The captivity was fulfilled in his days, and he saw the destruction of Jerusalem and its complete burning (Jer 38:14-39:10; 52:12-13; 2 Kgs 25:1-21).

49.6.0.en: 10 It was Ezekiel who saw the glorious vision, which was shown him upon the chariot of the cherubim. 11 For He made mention of the enemies under the figure of the rain, and directed them that went right. 12 And of the twelve prophets let the bones flourish out of their place; for they comforted Jacob, and delivered them by assured hope.

49.6.1.en: Ben Sira declared that God's care for the people while they were under chastening had not ceased. The people had become like the bones of the dead, but the prophets received grace from God to raise the dead spiritually, just as the bones of the dead Elisha raised the man who was cast into the grave.

49.6.2.en: Ezekiel himself saw the vision of glory; God showed it to him upon the chariot of the cherubim [8].

49.6.3.en: Ezekiel is regarded as a shining star among the prophets in the land of captivity. His book begins with the vision of the divine throne, so that God may assure His people that He longs for them to share with the heavenly ones in enjoying His glory; and on the other hand, that He has no need of the Temple which they defiled, nor of offerings and worship, unless their hearts are holy to Him, prepared for His dwelling. And the book ends with the glorious temple of the New Covenant. Thus the prophet Ezekiel prophesied in the land of captivity, opening the door of hope to his people.

49.6.4.en: He saw the vision of the dry bones that became alive and stood up as an exceeding great army (Ezek 37:8-10). Because the people were driven out of their homeland on account of their idolatrous abominations and their shedding of blood, their cities were turned into ruins in which no one dwelt, and they became like a place full of many bones, very dry. In other words, they became like an open grave holding lifeless bones! This is not a picture of the cities but rather of the people themselves, who were scattered in many places with a broken soul, and became like a valley of death containing dry bones that need someone to raise them from their death, gather them together again and give them life.

49.6.5.en: Ben Sira felt that the people had come to be in a state of death, indeed that they had become dry bones through their rejection of the divine wisdom and their preoccupation with vain wisdom; but the Lord alone is able to touch these dry bones, give them life, and make them stand upon their feet and set out toward the heavenly Jerusalem. This was fulfilled by the incarnation of the Wisdom of God and His offering of Himself as a sacrifice; and when He was laid in the tomb, He touched the dry bones that were in Hades and set out with them to Paradise.

49.6.6.en: O that the Lord would enter every heart as into a tomb, to take our souls to His Paradise!

49.6.7.en: For He made mention of His enemies in a thunderstorm, and did good to those who direct their ways uprightly [9].

49.6.8.en: Let the bones of the twelve indeed flourish out of their place, for they comforted[1] the people of Jacob, and delivered them with steadfast hope [10].

49.6.9.en: Ben Sira calls us to take care of the writings of the prophets, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the twelve minor prophets, as he highlighted before the role of prophets such as Elijah and Elisha.

49.7.0.en: 13 How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? For he was as a signet on the right hand. 14 So was Jesus the son of Josedec; for they in their days builded the house, and set up a holy people to the Lord, which was prepared for everlasting glory. 15 And among the elect was Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again.

49.7.1.en: Ben Sira mentioned three heroes of faith who built the house of the Lord and the wall of the city, and who cared for the word of God and worship.

49.7.2.en: The processions of return from the captivity were three.

49.7.3.en: The first procession was in 538/537 B.C. under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Sheshbazzar), the grandson of King Jehoiachin, and Jeshua the priest. Zerubbabel represented the civil authority, and Jeshua the priest represented the religious authority. Cyrus the Persian did not send Zerubbabel as a king with full freedom to act.

49.7.4.en: It is the procession of liberation from the devil and of ascent to the heavenly Jerusalem under the leadership of the Lord of glory Jesus, as King of kings and at the same time the heavenly High Priest, bearing kingship and priesthood at the same time.

49.7.5.en: The second procession was in 458 B.C. under the leadership of Ezra the scribe, who dealt with the problem of those married to pagan women (Ezra 7-10).

49.7.6.en: The third procession was in 445/444 B.C. under the leadership of Nehemiah the governor, who was concerned with building the wall; it was built in 52 days. The walls were dedicated, the Law was read, and the people enjoyed the joy of the Spirit (Neh 1-13). Zerubbabel stood out as a descendant of King David, as a type of Christ, the King of kings. In the second company Ezra the priest stood out as a type of the Word of God and the great High Priest, and in the last company Nehemiah, faithful in his work, stood out as a type of the Lord Christ, who is called the Faithful.

49.7.8.en: He is without doubt like a signet on the right hand [11].

49.7.9.en: He led the first company to Israel (Ezra 2:2); together with Jeshua and his brethren the priests he took part in building the altar for offering the burnt offerings and ordering the worship (Ezra 3:1-9). He was appointed governor and laid the foundation of the Temple (Zech 4:6-10). He labored for the rebuilding of the Temple, so it was called Zerubbabel's Temple, and the building remained standing until the year 20 B.C., when Herod rebuilt it anew.

49.7.10.en: So also Jeshua the son of Jozadak; in their days the house was built, and the holy temple of the Lord was set up, prepared for everlasting glory [12].

49.7.11.en: And the remembrance of Nehemiah is lasting; it was he who raised up for us the wall that was fallen, and set up for us the gates and the bars, and built the sites of our dwellings again [13].

49.7.12.en: He was born in captivity; he was not of royal descent like Zerubbabel, nor of priestly descent like Ezra, nor the holder of an administrative position like Daniel the prime minister; rather, his intense love for God and for his people made him a leader.

49.7.13.en: He used to taste the wine before the king so that the king might be assured that it was not poisoned. This position was distinguished in the Persian era. The king's cupbearer was often a eunuch, which explains why no mention is made of Nehemiah's family. Ezra preceded him to Jerusalem by about 13 years. Nehemiah was concerned with building the wall despite the opposition of the enemies to it; and he was also concerned with the inner building of the people. Then he returned to Susa, the capital, and did not remain there long, for he went back to Jerusalem as governor of Judah for at least 12 years. He represented true spiritual leadership. What occupied him was the sufferings of his brethren. He learned leadership through bended knees, silence, tears and crying out. He practiced prayer in every circumstance.

49.8.s.en: 5. The men of God before the Law

49.8.0.en: 16 But upon the earth was no man created like Enoch; for he was taken from the earth. 17 Neither was there a man born like unto Joseph, a governor of his brethren, a stay of the people. 18 His bones were regarded of the Lord, and after his death they prophesied. 19 Shem and Seth were in great honour among men, and so was Adam above every living thing in the creation.

49.8.1.en: No one was created upon the earth like Enoch, for he was taken up from the earth [14].

49.8.2.en: Now, lest the reader be occupied with the history of the heroes, Ben Sira wished to show that each of the heroes of faith has an excellence in a particular respect that differs from the rest of the heroes.

49.8.3.en: Enoch was worthy, by his godliness, of a unique friendship with God, so He took him from the earth to heaven.

49.8.4.en: And Joseph was worthy, by his love for his brothers and his not repaying them for their treachery against him, so he became the ruler of his brothers, who took his bones with them in the Exodus under the leadership of Moses.

49.8.5.en: And Shem covered his father Noah when he was uncovered because of drunkenness (Gen 9), and Seth was the secret of the consolation of his parents (Gen 4).

49.8.6.en: As for Adam, although he and his wife Eve sinned, we are indebted to him as the father of all humanity according to the flesh.

49.8.7.en: And no man was born like Joseph, the ruler of his brothers and the support of his people; and they cared for his bones [15].

49.8.8.en: The translation of Enoch from the earth is considered the planting of the seed of the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead and the enjoyment of the other life; and also Joseph's concern that his bones be carried to the Promised Land carries a hint of hope in the coming resurrection.

49.8.9.en: Shem and Seth were glorified among men, and Adam was above every living thing in creation [16].

49.8.10.en: Seth, a type of the Lord Christ: Many of the Fathers spoke of Seth from various aspects. St. Mar Jacob of Sarug recorded for us a special homily on Seth, in his poetic style that stirs the soul, in 140 lines. Through it the believer feels that God does not leave a believer in bitterness, but with the multitude of sufferings and their bitterness, His divine consolations increase in their sweetness. As St. Mar Jacob of Sarug shares with our first parents Adam and Eve the bitterness of their souls on account of the killing of Abel at the hands of his brother Cain, he touches the wondrous divine consolations that overflowed upon them at the birth of their son Seth. The secret of their consolation is not that God gave them a son in place of Abel and Cain, when they saw death for the first time in their lives and realized how the earthly body returns to the dust. They also saw Cain in great terror, fearing the animals and being frightened even of his own shadow. Rather, they saw in Seth the surpassing love of God and the consolations of heaven, and they understood divine mysteries that lifted their hearts as though to heaven. 1. Seth was a type of the incarnate Word of God, who gladdens humanity by His salvation. 2. Seth stands over against Cain, for the latter is the founder of the earthly city that leads man down toward the abyss, and the former is the founder of the heavenly city that lifts the depths of the believer to Paradise!

49.8.11.en: v O glorious Son, who resembles His Father as Seth (resembled) Adam, put upon my tongue the beauty of Your mystery, that I may speak of it.

49.8.12.en: O Son, who consoled Eve by Your mystery and removed her grief, stir my word with Your power that I may recount Your story.

49.8.13.en: I have suffered because of the grief that befell the house of Adam! My Lord, help me to speak of their consolation by means of radiant Seth.

49.8.14.en: I had spoken of the great suffering of Abel, and of the curses with which Cain was cursed by God.

49.8.15.en: I mentioned before you the sacrifices of the two sons of Adam, and the narrative proceeded to the reading according to its order.

49.8.16.en: I had also spoken of the lamentations of our mother Eve, and of the intensity of a mother's grief over her beloved.

49.8.17.en: Today it is needful for me to speak of their consolation, and by what cause they forgot their bitter afflictions.

49.8.18.en: Let me first recount what sufferings overtook them, and afterward I will return to the consolation that made them glad [2].

49.8.19.en: St. Mar Jacob of Sarug, inspired by Sirach 49

49.9.s.en: How great are Your shining stars!

49.9.0.en: v My soul blesses You for Your wondrous shining, O Sun of Righteousness.

49.9.1.en: In every generation many think as though the world has become utterly corrupt.

49.9.2.en: But You fill our hearts with the joy of hope in You.

49.9.3.en: You send forth Your light in the midst of darkness, and raise up from humanity radiant stars!

49.9.4.en: In the last period of the kingdom of Judah, corrupt kings succeeded one another, who devoted their lives to the corruption of Your people!

49.9.5.en: You raised up King Josiah as though he were a censer sending forth pure incense that bears Your fragrant aroma.

49.9.6.en: When one speaks of him, his mouth becomes a spring of sweet honey.

49.9.7.en: And when we look at the work of Your grace in him, we realize that You raise up musicians who fill the world with the joy of the Spirit!

49.9.8.en: v In the bitterness of the captivity, the powers of darkness could not keep the soul of Ezekiel from enjoying the glories of Your divine throne.
